extra.message: Single Shared Token Guarding All Dangerous Ops Routes — If the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN is compromised, the attacker gains unrestricted access to all critical RCE, file write, and data exfiltration endpoints in the /ops/* router. [verified: The _wrk_gate at line 16-18 is the sole protection for all 16 ops routes using a single shared INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN from environment with no rate limiting; if the token is leaked via env disclosure, logs, or config management, every RCE-capable endpoint becomes accessible.]

Arbitrary code execution via eval() on user input — Remote code execution on the server. Full system compromise. [verified: User-supplied `expr` is passed to eval() at line 76; the restricted __builtins__ dict is trivially bypassed through Python object attribute chains to reach os or subprocess.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 string concatenation — Remote code execution on the server via Jinja2 sandbox escape. Full system compromise. [verified: User-supplied `fragment` is concatenated into a Jinja2 template string at line 117 without sanitization; SSTI payloads like {{config}} or class hierarchy chains achieve RCE via sandbox escape.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 String Concatenation — Remote code execution; server compromise, data exfiltration, config disclosure. [verified: User-supplied `fragment` is concatenated into a Jinja2 template string at line 117 without sanitization; SSTI payloads like {{config}} or class hierarchy chains achieve RCE via sandbox escape.]

Path traversal leading to arbitrary file write via user-controlled filename — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem. Can be escalated to RCE by overwriting crontabs, application code, or startup scripts. [verified: User-supplied `name` is used directly as a file path component at line 123 with no traversal sanitization; attackers can write arbitrary files outside BASE_EXPORT_DIR via ../ sequences, enabling RCE via cron or code overwrite.]

Command injection via os.system with unsanitized user input — Remote code execution on the server as the application user. Full system compromise. [verified: User-supplied `host` query parameter is directly concatenated into os.system() at line 146 with no escaping; shell metacharacters like `;` or `$()` inject arbitrary commands for RCE.]

OS Command Injection via String Interpolation in ping Command — Remote command execution on the host operating system; full server compromise. [verified: User-supplied `host` query parameter is directly concatenated into os.system() at line 146 with no escaping; shell metacharacters like `;` or `$()` inject arbitrary commands for RCE.]

Pickle deserialization of untrusted request data enables RCE — Remote code execution on the server by sending a crafted pickle payload. Full system compromise. [verified: User-controlled request body reaches pickle.loads() at line 61 with no sanitization; the _wrk_gate controls access but a malicious pickle payload enables RCE via __reduce__.]

Path traversal in stash endpoint enables arbitrary file write with sensitive PII data — Attacker can write arbitrary JSON files outside the intended directory while server stores SSN and credit card numbers in plaintext at a predictable location. [verified: User-controlled `ref` at line 69 allows ../ traversal to write JSON files to arbitrary locations while the endpoint writes mock SSN (111-22-3333) and credit card (4111111111111111) in plaintext at line 71.]

Sensitive Data (SSN/Credit Card) Written to Disk in dispatch-stash-241 — Exposure of sensitive PII (SSN) and financial data (credit card numbers) on the filesystem. An attacker with filesystem access can read this data. [verified: User-controlled `ref` at line 69 allows ../ traversal to write JSON files to arbitrary locations while the endpoint writes mock SSN (111-22-3333) and credit card (4111111111111111) in plaintext at line 71.]

NoSQL injection via user-controlled MongoDB filter object — Attacker can manipulate MongoDB queries to extract sensitive data from arbitrary collections, bypass intended query constraints. [verified: User-supplied JSON is used directly as a MongoDB filter at line 133 with no sanitization; attackers can inject $gt, $regex, $where operators to extract unauthorized data or perform blind injection.]

XML External Entity (XXE) injection with DTD loading and network access enabled — Attacker can read arbitrary server files, perform SSRF attacks, or cause denial of service via entity expansion (Billion Laughs). [verified: lxml XMLParser at line 139 enables DTD loading and entity resolution without network restrictions; an attacker can read local files or perform SSRF via a malicious XML document with external entities.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Brute-force password guessing, user enumeration via repeated requests, and denial of service via password reset spam. No protection against automated attacks on authentication endpoints. [verified: All four auth endpoints (login line 415, register line 450, password-reset/request line 500, password-reset/confirm line 522) lack rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection. Aggregated duplicate of idx 0/2/4.]

Hardcoded secure=False on Registration Session Cookie Overrides Global Configuration — Registration session cookies transmitted in cleartext over HTTP; session hijacking for newly registered users. [verified: Same code as idx 3: registration at main.py:490 hardcodes secure=False, overriding any COOKIE_SECURE=true configuration. Duplicate finding.]

Password Reset Token Leaked in API Response and Log File — An attacker can obtain the plaintext reset token and change any user's password, gaining full unauthorized access to their account. [verified: At main.py:512–513 the raw reset token is leaked in API response when APP_ENV != 'production'. Additionally at main.py:509 the token is written in plaintext to local_mocks/password_resets.log on disk.]

CSV formula injection in export_incidents allows spreadsheet formula execution — An attacker (including any authenticated customer) can inject spreadsheet formulas into the incidents CSV export. When an admin opens the file in Excel or LibreOffice Calc, formulas execute — enabling data exfiltration via WEBSERVICE/DDE, command execution, or other malicious actions within the spreadsheet context. [verified: Customer-created incidents store customer_summary verbatim (main.py:1076). The export endpoint at main.py:1494 passes it to csv.DictWriter which does not escape leading =, +, -, @ — when an admin opens the CSV in Excel, injected formulas execute.]

Authorization header logged in plaintext — Credentials or bearer tokens in the Authorization header are persisted to application logs, enabling credential theft if logs are compromised. [verified: The Authorization header value is written to application logs at line 33 via logger.warning(); credentials or bearer tokens are exposed to anyone with log access (SIEM, file read).]

Log Injection and Sensitive Credential Exposure in Log Output — Log poisoning (injection of fake audit records); exposure of Authorization header secrets in log files accessible to insiders or via log-monitoring systems. [verified: The Authorization header value is written to application logs at line 33 via logger.warning(); credentials or bearer tokens are exposed to anyone with log access (SIEM, file read).]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe filter on user-controlled input — Attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the victim's browser when they visit the crafted URL, leading to session theft, CSRF bypass, or phishing. [verified: User-supplied `card` is rendered with the |safe filter at line 87, bypassing Jinja2 auto-escaping; arbitrary HTML/JS injection is possible though XSS exploitation requires the victim's browser to send the x-internal-token header.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 safe filter in dispatch-tile-327 — Attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript into the response, leading to session theft, credential harvesting, or actions performed in the victim's browser context. [verified: User-supplied `card` is rendered with the |safe filter at line 87, bypassing Jinja2 auto-escaping; arbitrary HTML/JS injection is possible though XSS exploitation requires the victim's browser to send the x-internal-token header.]

Disabled TLS certificate verification for outbound HTTPS connection — Man-in-the-middle attacker on the network path can intercept, modify, or redirect the outbound HTTPS connection undetected. [verified: TLS certificate verification is disabled at line 158 via ssl._create_unverified_context() for an outbound HTTPS request at line 159; a MITM attacker on the network can intercept and modify the response undetected, though the target URL is hardcoded.]

Disabled SSL/TLS Certificate Verification in dispatch-drift-649 — Man-in-the-middle attack vulnerability. An attacker on the network can intercept, decrypt, and modify the outbound HTTPS request/response without detection. [verified: TLS certificate verification is disabled at line 158 via ssl._create_unverified_context() for an outbound HTTPS request at line 159; a MITM attacker on the network can intercept and modify the response undetected, though the target URL is hardcoded.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints Enabling Brute-Force — Offline and online brute-force of user passwords; unlimited credential stuffing; enumeration via registration endpoint. [verified: Login and register endpoints at main.py:415 and main.py:450 have no rate-limiting decorator, throttling middleware, or CAPTCHA. Duplicate of idx 0 and 2 combined.]

User enumeration via distinct registration error message — Attacker can probe email addresses to discover registered user accounts, enabling targeted phishing or credential-stuffing attacks. [verified: Register endpoint at main.py:450–454 returns distinct 409 'An account with this email already exists' vs proceeding for new emails, enabling email enumeration via response differentiation.]

Missing Secure Flag on Session Cookie Defaulting to False — Session hijacking via passive network eavesdropping (MITM); attacker captures the cleartext session cookie over HTTP. [verified: Login endpoint at main.py:429 reads COOKIE_SECURE defaulting to 'false' (line 429). If the env var is unset, the session cookie lacks the Secure flag and is transmitted over HTTP.]

Missing rate limiting on password reset endpoint — Attacker can flood users with reset emails or abuse the endpoint for reconnaissance without any request throttling. [verified: Password-reset/request at main.py:500 has no rate limiting. An attacker can spam reset emails to any registered user address without throttling.]

Cross-region customer PII exposure to dispatchers — Dispatchers can exfiltrate all customer PII (name, email, phone, billing_ref) from other regions/tenants [verified: list_customers (line 627) returns ALL customers via customer_out() for dispatchers with no region-based filtering, whereas other endpoints like list_locations and list_jobs apply region scoping for dispatchers via ServiceLocation.region_id.]

Stored CSV Formula Injection via export_routes company_name — Attacker can achieve arbitrary code execution or data exfiltration on analyst workstations that open the exported CSV in spreadsheet software [verified: export_routes writes job.customer.company_name into CSV via csv.DictWriter with no sanitization of formula-injection prefixes (=, +, -, @). company_name is stored verbatim from CSV import (line 1560) with no validation for formula injection, and csv_response() does not escape these prefixes.]

Stored CSV Formula Injection via export_completions billing_ref and company_name — Attacker can achieve arbitrary code execution or data exfiltration on analyst workstations that open the exported CSV in spreadsheet software [verified: export_completions writes job.customer.company_name (line 1449) and job.customer.billing_ref (line 1456) via csv_response() with no sanitization of formula-injection prefixes. Both fields originate from CSV import where they are stored verbatim with no prefix stripping.]

Information disclosure via verbose error messages in CSV import — Attacker learns internal schema, file paths, and database structure from verbose exception messages returned after malformed CSV uploads [verified: import_csv catches generic Exception and appends str(exc) verbatim to the returned errors list (line ~1582), leaking SQL constraint names, column details, and internal paths to an authenticated attacker who crafts malformed CSV uploads.]

Hardcoded integration API key in seed data enables unauthorized job status changes — Unauthorized modification of any job's status (including completing, cancelling, or re-opening jobs); bypass of intended workflow transitions; potential supply-chain injection if job status triggers downstream actions. [verified: Hardcoded API key 'fd_demo_status_key_please_rotate' in seed.py:309 is published in README.md and tests; any instance running seed data accepts this key for /api/integrations/status-update with no compensating rotation or expiration control. Severity reduced to medium because the seed is not auto-loaded on production startup and the key name itself recommends rotation.]

Information Disclosure via Verbose Error Messages in dispatch-manifest-pulse-079 — Leaks internal file paths (BASE_EXPORT_DIR), exception class details, and user input reflection, aiding attackers in reconnaissance. [verified: Line 27 returns the full exception message (containing user-controlled `lot_ref` and server path BASE_EXPORT_DIR) plus exception class name in the response, leaking internal server details.]

Open redirect via user-controlled redirect target — Attacker can redirect victims to phishing sites or malicious downloads from a trusted domain, bypassing URL reputation filters. [verified: User-supplied `lane` is passed directly to RedirectResponse at line 39 with no URL validation; open redirect is possible but requires the x-internal-token header, significantly reducing phishing utility.]

Reflected CORS origin with credentials enables cross-origin data theft — Any malicious website can make credentialed requests to this endpoint on behalf of an authenticated user and read the response, leading to data exfiltration. [verified: The Origin header is reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin at line 103 with credentials enabled at line 104; however, auth is via x-internal-token header (not cookies), so browser auto-credential flow does not apply, limiting cross-origin data theft.]

Reflective CORS with Credentials Enabled on Dynamic Origin — Cross-origin data theft; authenticated endpoints on this origin can be called from any malicious website, exfiltrating session-protected data. [verified: The Origin header is reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin at line 103 with credentials enabled at line 104; however, auth is via x-internal-token header (not cookies), so browser auto-credential flow does not apply, limiting cross-origin data theft.]

File content-type validation trusts unauthenticated client header — Attacker can upload files with arbitrary content while claiming an allowed MIME type; combined with the broad 'application/octet-stream' allowance, any file type is technically permitted. [verified: The MIME check at main.py:975 trusts the client's Content-Type header and allows application/octet-stream, making the check trivially bypassable. However, the randomized stored filename (token_urlsafe(18)) and dedicated UPLOAD_DIR prevent RCE, limiting real impact.]

Race condition in CSV import job reference generation — Concurrent CSV imports generate duplicate job references causing data corruption, import failures, and uniqueness constraint violations [verified: The count()+local-counter pattern for job references (line ~1566) is a TOCTOU race condition — concurrent imports can see the same base count and generate duplicate references — but the unique constraint on Job.reference prevents silent data corruption, causing only import errors.]

Webhook secret stored in plaintext in database — Database compromise or SQL injection reveals plaintext webhook secrets, enabling an attacker to forge webhook payloads or impersonate the application to downstream services. [verified: WebhookEndpoint.secret is stored as plaintext String(120) with no encryption-at-rest. However, the secret is never returned by any API endpoint (webhook_out excludes it) and the system never actually delivers webhooks — test_webhook only records 'mock-delivered locally' — so the plaintext secret provides no practical forging/impersonation capability.]

User/Account Enumeration via Distinct Error Messages on Handle Lookup — Enumeration of valid operational handles ('north', 'south') enabling targeted attacks. [verified: Line 93 returns 404 for unknown handles while known handles proceed to the verifier check at line 94, enabling enumeration of the two valid handle names ("north", "south") via HTTP status code differences.]

Information Disclosure via Handle Enumeration in dispatch-hint-559 — Attacker can enumerate valid system handles ('north', 'south') by observing the distinct error messages returned for existing vs non-existing handles. [verified: Line 93 returns 404 for unknown handles while known handles proceed to the verifier check at line 94, enabling enumeration of the two valid handle names ("north", "south") via HTTP status code differences.]
